title: Intraspecific variations in the cranium of Iguanodon (Ornithopoda: Iguanodontidae), with comments on functional and evolutionary patterns
content:
Abstract
Many characters employed in taxonomic and phylogenetic study of iguanodontian ornithopods are found in the cranium. However, they might be highly intraspecifically variable within species, both individually and ontogenetically. Sources of variation have been widely studied in the crania of Late Cretaceous hadrosaurids but less in those of non-hadrosaurid iguanodontians. Herein, we present novel research on observable and measurable variations in the cranium of Iguanodon, based on the study of several perinates (egg-sized to 1 m in body length) of Iguanodon galvensis. Individual variations in these perinates, as well as potential ontogenetic traits, have been described and quantified by comparing them with other skeletally immature and mature specimens of both I. galvensis and Iguanodon bernissartensis. As a result, we observed that some developmental changes in individual bones were consequences of a general enlargement of the preorbital region, a proportional reduction of the ocular orbit, and an increase in tooth number in both maxillae and dentaries, among others. According to the macro- and microwear patterns of their teeth, the perinates had a shearing feeding apparatus that also moved transversely and propalinally (i.e. rostrocaudally) during mandibular adduction. Finally, cranial ontogeny in Iguanodon supports the hypothesis that peramorphosis (i.e. a descendant species develops beyond its ancestor) played a key role in the morphological evolution of the ornithopod cranium.
